# Renovation Log Bathroom

## Overview
This was a full rip-out and refit of the only bathroom in the flat, a small room about two and a half metres by two, and it took a little over two weeks of evenings and weekends with a couple of days off work at the end. The old suite was a dated avocado affair that had been there since the flat was built and had never worked well: the bath was too short, the basin too small and the shower hung off the wall in a way that soaked the floor every time. The plan was to keep the layout broadly as it was, since moving the soil pipe would have ballooned the cost, but replace everything else and add proper tanking and a decent extractor. I did the bulk of the work myself and called in a plumber for the things that needed signing off. Two and a half thousand euros all in, which I think is reasonable for the state it was in. This is the log I kept as I went, mostly so I would remember the lessons for the next room. I did most of the work around a full-time job, which meant early mornings and late evenings, and I would not do that again in a hurry.

## Week One
The first morning was the worst of it. I started by ripping out the old suite, taking the bath panels off and cutting the old pipework free, and the whole thing came away in a cloud of dust and the most appalling smell of old sealant and trapped damp that had been sitting under the bath for decades. I filled a whole skip by lunchtime with the old bath, the basin, the toilet, the tiles off the walls and the rotted boarding behind them. The skip sat on the drive for the week and the neighbours were very patient about it. Once the room was bare I could see the damage properly, and it was clear the old sealant had been hiding a slow leak that had been going for years.

The floor joists underneath were the first real job. Two of them, near the soil pipe, had gone soft where the leak had reached them, and one had a notch cut into it by some earlier plumber that left it weaker than it should be. I sistered new timber alongside the soft ones and bolted the pair together every few hundred millimetres, then treated the lot against damp and rot. It was slow, awkward work in a small space, and it ate most of the second day. The rest of the joists were sound once the wet boarding came up, which was a relief, because replacing a joist end that sits in the wall is a far bigger job than sistering a new one alongside.

The plumbing went in next, and this is the part I was glad to hand to someone who knew what they were doing. The plumber reran the hot and cold feeds in plastic rather than the old copper, moved the shower valve up to a sensible height and fitted a proper isolating valve on every line so the next person can work on one thing without draining the whole system. The soil pipe stayed where it was, which saved a fortune, and the new toilet sits squarely over it. He pressure-tested everything and left it capped for the tiling. I ran the new extractor duct out through the wall at the same time, since it is far easier to cut that hole before the boarding goes up than after.

With the pipework done I turned to the walls. I took the old plaster back to the brick where it had blown and then fixed backer board over the whole wet area, screwed to the studs at close centres rather than the occasional fixing the old plasterboard had used. The backer board is the bit that carries the weight of the tiles and keeps the water out of the wall, so it is not a place to save money or time. I taped and sealed the joints with the proper waterproof tape and painted the lot with a tanking compound, two coats, letting each dry before the next. The floor got the same treatment around the shower and the toilet, turned up the wall a little at the edges to form a proper tray. It looked ugly at that stage, a grey and beige patchwork, but it would all be hidden.

Then came the tile layout, and I spent an entire evening on it before fixing a single tile. I marked a centre line on the back wall and worked the rows out from there, so the cuts would fall at both edges rather than leaving one thin sliver in a corner. I checked how the tiles would meet the window reveal and the top of the shower, because getting those junctions wrong is what makes a job look amateur even when the tiling itself is neat. I drew the layout on the wall in pencil and lived with it overnight. The last decision was the tiles themselves, and I settled on large-format porcelain to cut down on the number of grout lines and make the small room feel bigger.

By the end of the first week the room was stripped, re-framed, plumbed, boarded, tanked and roughly laid out, and the tiles were stacked in the hall waiting. The tiles are 60 by 30 cm and go on with a 10 mm notched trowel, which gives a bed deep enough to level out the slight unevenness in the walls. I set the first row on a batten, worked upward in small sections, and back-buttered every single tile rather than relying on the combed adhesive alone, which is the trick that stops a large tile from sounding hollow when you tap it weeks later. That evening I stood in the doorway and looked at the first few rows climbing the wall, and for the first time the room looked like it might actually work.

## Week Two
The second week was the finishing, and it took longer than the first in some ways because the fiddly work cannot be rushed. I grouted the walls once the adhesive had fully set, working in small areas and sponging off before the grout went hard, which is a two-person job if ever there was one. The silicone came next, a neat bead along the bath and the shower tray and every internal corner, done slowly with masking tape so the line stayed straight. I hate silicone and the tape made the difference between a clean joint and a mess. The extractor went in last, wired to come on with the light and run on for a few minutes after, which is the standard way and the right one. Then the first shower, and the water ran hot and strong and the floor stayed dry, which after two weeks of work was the best thing I had felt in a long time. The grouting took two evenings because I could only do a couple of square metres at a time before it started to set, and the silicone took most of another. I painted the ceiling and the window reveal once everything else was done, which I had left until last on purpose so the dust from the tiling would not ruin it. The extractor duct needed a bit of fettling to sit flush with the outside wall, and I sealed around it with the same silicone as the corners. Standing under hot water in a room I had built myself was worth every late night.

## Costs
The whole job came to 2500 EUR, which I kept a tally of as I went. The tiles and adhesive were the biggest single line, a little over six hundred, with the sanitaryware close behind at around five hundred for the bath, basin, toilet and the brassware. The plumber's time and the parts came to about four hundred, money well spent given what he reran. The skip, the timber for the joists and the backer board added a few hundred more, and the tools I bought along the way, a decent trowel, a tile cutter and a wet saw, took the rest. I owned the drill and the levels already, which helped. I kept every receipt in a folder as I went, which is the only reason the total is exact rather than a guess. The skip was the one cost I underestimated, coming in a little higher than I had allowed, while the tiles came in under what the showroom had quoted. If I had paid someone to do the whole job the figure would have been three or four times what it cost me in materials and evenings.

## Notes
The lesson I would pass on is to sort the pipework and the boarding before you think about tiles, because everything else is easy once those are right and impossible to fix afterwards. I would also never again do silicone without masking tape. The tanking added a day and I would do it every time. If I did the room again I would move the soil pipe and gain the space, but that is a job for a plumber and a bigger budget than this one. The room has held up well since, no leaks, no hollow tiles, and the extractor keeps the mirror clear in a way the old fan never did. I would take the extra day for tanking every time, and I would buy the wet saw at the start rather than hiring one halfway through.
